rules.title: Prohibition on Coordinated Pricing Algorithms for Rent/Occupancy Setting
rules.requirement: In Berkeley, it is unlawful for anyone to sell, license, or provide to a Berkeley landlord, and unlawful for a landlord to use, a 'coordinated pricing algorithm' that uses nonpublic competitor data (actual rents, occupancy, lease dates, etc., less than 90 days old) shared across competing landlords to calculate or recommend rents, fees, or occupancy levels for residential units. The law does not cap or otherwise set the amount of rent a landlord may charge; it only bans the algorithmic coordination mechanism.
rules.key_value: $1,000 per violation (civil penalty)

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to all residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley; the ordinance text states no exemption based on building size, year built, or owner-occupancy.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to: (a) aggregated/anonymized data reports/studies that do not recommend rent, fee or occupancy figures; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under government affordable-housing guidelines; (c) products/processes used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research/testing/training of software (including ML model training), so long as competitor data is not used as a live input when a recommendation is actually calculated and provided to a landlord.
rules.interaction: This Chapter expressly does not regulate the amount of rent a landlord may charge; it solely bans the sale/use of coordinated pricing algorithms. It operates alongside, and is distinct from, Berkeley's separate rent stabilization and just-cause eviction ordinances.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley.
rules.conflict_note: Document shows the ordinance was 'passed to print' on 2025-11-18 by the Berkeley City Council; the source filename indicates a second-reading/adoption item dated 2025-12-02. The effective_date of 2026-01-01 is inferred (adoption date + standard ~30-day operative period for Berkeley ordinances) because the document itself does not state a final adoption or operative date.
rules.penalty: City Attorney may bring a civil action for damages, injunctive relief, restitution of illegal profits, and/or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation (each month and each unit is a separate violation), with mandatory attorney's fees/costs to the City Attorney if prevailing. An aggrieved tenant may separately sue for injunctive relief, damages, and/or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation, with mandatory attorney's fees/costs to the tenant if prevailing; a lease clause limiting a prevailing tenant's right to fees is unenforceable.

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Berkeley rental housing providers may not ask about, require disclosure of, or use an applicant's or tenant's criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decisions to rent, renew, or terminate a tenancy. Landlords also may not charge a higher deposit or rent, deny addition of an immediate family member, or disqualify someone from a rental assistance program (e.g., Section 8) because of criminal history, subject to listed exemptions. If a landlord takes adverse action based on criminal history, it must give the applicant/tenant written notice and an opportunity to respond.

coverage_conditions.notes: Exemption applies to owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as a primary residence; other exemptions (not building-related) include lifetime registered sex offenders, limited public housing/Section 8 exemptions, units subject to an owner move-back agreement under BMC 13.76.130 A.9, and units where an existing tenant seeks to sublet or add/replace roommates.

rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offender registrants; public housing/Section 8 properties (limited exemptions); owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as primary residence; units under an owner move-back agreement per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenant(s) seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates.

rules.title: Ban on coercive use/distribution of common pricing algorithms (Cartwright Act)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a 'common pricing algorithm' as part of an anticompetitive conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use/distribute such an algorithm to coerce another party into setting or adopting the price or commercial term it recommends for the same or similar products or services in California.
rules.exemptions: Subsection (c) states the section does not impair or limit the applicability of other antitrust laws; this is a savings clause, not a substantive carve-out.
rules.interaction: Adds to the Cartwright Act (Bus. & Prof. Code pt. 2) a general-application ban on coordinated 'common pricing algorithm' use/distribution; a companion provision (Sec. 16756.1, also added by this bill) relaxes the pleading standard for Cartwright Act complaints alleging such conduct.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.conflict_note: This is a general antitrust prohibition applicable to any industry's use of coordinated pricing software; the bill text itself never mentions rental housing, landlords, or tenants. It is included here only because a 'common pricing algorithm' as broadly defined (any software using competitor data to recommend/align/set a price for 'the same or similar products or services') would encompass algorithmic rent-setting tools (e.g., revenue-management software used by landlords) when used in a coercive or conspiratorial manner; applicability to the rental-housing market specifically is inferred, not stated.

rules.title: Maximum Tenant Screening Fee (Annual State Cap)
rules.requirement: California landlords may charge a prospective tenant a screening/application fee only up to an annually-adjusted statutory cap; for 2026 the maximum is $68.96. The fee may only cover the cost of obtaining things like a consumer credit report and processing the application, unused portions must be refunded, and the fee cannot be charged if no unit is actually available or (unless using a first-qualified-applicant policy) to applicants not ultimately selected.

rules.title: Just Cause Requirement for Termination of Residential Tenancy
rules.requirement: After a tenant (or all tenants, if added later) has lawfully occupied a rental unit for 12 months (or 24 months in some multi-tenant situations), the landlord cannot end the tenancy without a legally recognized 'just cause' reason, which must be stated in the written termination notice. For no-fault terminations (e.g., owner move-in, demolition/substantial remodel, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate), the landlord must also pay the tenant one month's rent as relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent.

coverage_conditions.notes: Also exempt: transient/tourist hotels; nonprofit hospital/religious/extended-care/licensed elderly or adult residential care facilities; college dormitories and K-12 schools; residences where tenant shares bath/kitchen with a resident owner; real property alienable separately from any other unit where the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member (contingent on a specific written exemption notice); and deed-restricted/subsidized affordable housing for very low, low, or moderate income households.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to: transient/tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed elderly residential care facility, or adult residential facility; dormitories owned/operated by higher-ed institutions or K-12 schools; housing where tenant shares bath/kitchen with an owner who lives on site; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than 2 units/bedrooms (incl. ADU/JADU) and mobilehomes; a 2-unit property where the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); property alienable separate from title to any other unit where the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member (subject to a required exemption notice); and deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing for very low/low/moderate income households. Also excludes mobilehome homeowners (as opposed to renters); curable lease violations require a prior notice-and-cure opportunity.
rules.interaction: Local just-cause ordinances adopted on or before September 1, 2019 control instead of this section. Local ordinances adopted or amended after that date control only if they are 'more protective' (consistent with this section, further limiting termination reasons or providing higher relocation amounts or additional protections, with a binding local finding of greater protectiveness). Local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective than this section are not enforced unless this section is repealed. A property cannot be subject to both a local just-cause ordinance and this section at the same time.
rules.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy
rules.conflict_note: The document states this section 'shall become operative on April 1, 2024' (subd. rules.penalty: A termination notice issued in violation of this section is void. An owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation of this section is liable to the tenant for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs (in the court's discretion), and up to three times actual damages (plus possible punitive damages) for willful, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious conduct. The Attorney General or city/county counsel may seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: Statewide annual rent increase cap (AB 1482 / SB 567)
rules.requirement: An owner of residential real property cannot raise the rent on a covered unit by more than 5% plus the local change in the cost of living (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, and can only impose up to two such increases within that 12-month period. The cap does not apply to the initial rent set for a new tenancy once prior tenants have vacated.

coverage_conditions.notes: Excludes deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories/K-12 school housing, housing subject to a stricter local rent-control ordinance, housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years, single-family homes/condos alienable separately from title where the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member (and required notice is given), owner-occupied duplexes, and mobilehome homeowners (as opposed to mobilehome space renters).

rules.exemptions: Deed-restricted affordable housing; dormitories owned/operated by higher-education institutions or K-12 schools; housing subject to a local rent/price-control ordinance under Costa-Hawkins (Civ. Code § 1954.50 et seq.) that caps increases below this section's limit; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the prior 15 years (unless a mobilehome); single-family residences/condos alienable separately from other units where the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member and required statutory notice is given; a two-unit property where the owner occupies one unit as a principal residence; mobilehome homeowners under Civ. rules.interaction: This section neither expands nor limits the authority of local governments to adopt or maintain local rent/price control under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (Civ. rules.title: Restrictions on Use of Criminal History in Tenant Screening
rules.requirement: A housing provider may check an applicant's criminal history, but may not rely on arrests that did not lead to conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or juvenile justice records, and may not impose a blanket ban excluding all applicants with any criminal history. Any denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and to the health and safety of others, considering the nature/severity of the offense and time elapsed.
rules.exemptions: Arrests without conviction, sealed or expunged records, and juvenile-justice-system records cannot be considered; blanket bans on all applicants with any criminal history are prohibited.
rules.quoted_span: Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system. Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.

rules.title: Income-standard and credit-history screening restrictions for rental applicants (Gov. Code § 12955)
rules.requirement: Landlords may not use a financial or income standard for rental housing that fails to count the combined income of unmarried co-applicants the same way it would count married applicants' combined income. When an applicant has a government rent subsidy, the landlord's income-eligibility standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant personally pays, and if the landlord uses the applicant's credit history, it must let the applicant instead provide alternative proof of ability to pay (e.g., benefit records, pay stubs, bank statements) and reasonably consider that evidence.
rules.exemptions: Does not limit a housing provider's ability to request information to verify employment, request landlord references, or verify identity; making a written or oral inquiry about the level or source of a person's income is not itself discrimination.
rules.interaction: This provision (subd. (o), added/amended by SB 267, Stats. 2023 Ch. 776) applies specifically where there is a government rent subsidy; the aggregate-income rule (subd. (n)) applies more generally to rental income standards.

rules.conflict_note: The document shows subd. (n)'s aggregate-income rule and subd. (o)'s credit-history/subsidy rule as part of the same section; only the 2023 amendment (SB 267, effective 2024-01-01, adding/revising subd. (o)) has a stated effective date in this text, so the original effective date of subd. (n) is not confirmed here.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent (with limited exceptions)
rules.requirement: A landlord generally cannot demand or receive a security deposit worth more than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent. Narrow exceptions allow higher deposits for small landlords, long-term leases, and in certain service-member cases, and deposits must be itemized and returned within 21 days of move-out.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent (up to 2 months' rent for small landlords: natural persons/LLCs of natural persons owning ≤2 rental properties totaling ≤4 units)

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to residential rental agreements where the property is used as the tenant's dwelling. The higher 2-month deposit cap applies only if the landlord is a natural person (or an LLC whose members are all natural persons) who owns no more than two residential rental properties collectively containing no more than four dwelling units.

rules.exemptions: Does not prohibit an advance payment of 6+ months' rent if the lease term is 6 months or longer. A landlord meeting the small-landlord criteria (natural person/family-trust or all-natural-person LLC owning ≤2 properties/≤4 units) may charge up to 2 months' rent, except this higher amount is not allowed against service members. Service members may be charged a higher-than-standard deposit only with written disclosure, and the extra amount must be refunded after 6 months of non-delinquent residency. The one-month cap (as applicable before July 1, 2024) does not apply to deposits collected or demanded before that date. Agreed, separately-paid charges for optional alterations requested by the tenant are not counted as 'security.'

rules.penalty: Bad faith claim or retention of a security deposit (or bad faith demand of replacement security) can subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the deposit amount, in addition to actual damages.

rules.title: No-Fault Eviction Relocation Assistance Under the RSO & JCO
rules.requirement: Landlords evicting a tenant for an enumerated not-at-fault reason (owner/family/manager occupancy, demolition/conversion/removal from rental use, government order to vacate, HUD-ordered vacation, residential hotel conversion, conversion to affordable housing, or demolition/conversion to condos/hotels/commercial use) from a unit covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or Just Cause Ordinance (JCO) must pay relocation assistance per unit and file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD before serving the termination notice, with a copy of the notice filed with LAHD within 3 days of service. Relocation amounts (effective 7/1/2026-6/30/2027) range from $11,000 (eligible tenant, <3 years) to $27,400 (qualified tenant, 3+ years or low income), paid within 15 days of the notice, and increase every July 1.

A landlord may offset a tenant's accumulated unpaid rent against relocation assistance owed, except where the termination is required by a government order to vacate or comply with an unpermitted-dwelling order.

rules.title: Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (Citywide JCO)
rules.requirement: Landlords of most residential rental units in the City of Los Angeles that are NOT regulated by the City's Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) may terminate a tenancy only for an enumerated just cause, once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired (whichever comes first). At-fault causes (no relocation assistance owed) include failure to pay rent, uncured lease violations, nuisance or property damage, illegal use of the unit, failure to renew a similar rental agreement, denying the landlord reasonable access, or an unapproved subtenant remaining after the lease ends. No-fault causes (owner/immediate-family move-in, required resident-manager move-in, demolition/permanent removal from the rental market/conversion to non-residential use, government order to vacate, HUD sale of the property, conversion/demolition of a residential hotel, or conversion to affordable housing) require the landlord to pay the tenant relocation assistance. Separately, effective March 27, 2023, a landlord in an RSO or JCO unit may not evict a tenant for unpaid rent unless the amount owed exceeds the HUD Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size. Landlords must register covered units annually with LAHD, display the Registration Certificate, post a Notice of Right to Counsel (beginning August 20, 2025), and provide/post a Notice of Renters' Protections for tenancies beginning or renewing on or after January 27, 2023. All eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days of service.

coverage_conditions.notes: Can apply to buildings newer than October 1, 1978 (unlike the RSO) and can apply to a property with only one single-family dwelling. Exemptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity/sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless facilities or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers, and some properties owned by HACLA or government entities.

rules.exemptions: Transient hotels; licensed care facilities; fraternity or sorority houses; an owner's roommate; cooperatives under certain circumstances; some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term substance-abuse treatment centers; some properties owned by HACLA or the government; units already covered by the City's RSO (covered by RSO just-cause rules instead); tenancies under 6 months where the original lease has not expired.
rules.interaction: The JCO does not itself regulate rent increase amounts; rent increases in non-RSO buildings may instead be governed by state law (AB 1482 / Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12).

rules.title: Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) – Demolition for New Construction Relocation & Occupant Protections
rules.requirement: For 'Protected Units' demolished for new construction, the landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict or Notice of Intent to Withdraw with LAHD, serve tenants written notice, and provide occupant protections including the right to relocation, the right to remain in the unit up to 6 months before construction begins (with 6-month move-out notice), the right to return to the unit if demolition does not proceed, a right of first refusal to the new building for some tenants, and tenant notification requirements. Lower-income households must be paid enhanced relocation (Chart B); above-low-income households receive RSO/JCO Chart A amounts. The owner must choose one of three compliance options (standardized payment, comparable replacement unit, or individualized relocation) and pay the highest amount required by State and City law.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies only to 'Protected Units' being demolished for the purpose of new construction, where demolition/withdrawal filing occurs within 5 years of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict. Protected Units include: units subject (now or within the past 5 years) to a rent-restriction covenant/ordinance/law for lower/very-low income persons; units subject to any form of rent or price control (including all RSO units) within the past 5 years; units rented by lower/very-low income households within the past 5 years; or units withdrawn under the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

rules.interaction: The RPO codifies and expands the State's Housing Crisis Act (HCA, Cal. Gov't Code § 66300 et seq., originally enacted via SB 330 and later updated by SB 8 and AB 1218); the landlord must pay the higher of the RSO/JCO (Chart A) or RPO (Chart B) amount, and RSO/JCO amounts must also be enhanced for lower-income tenants under the HCA regardless of RPO applicability.

replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.
rules.penalty: Failure to comply with the RPO may result in financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.

rules.title: 14-Day Notice to Quit and Cure Right for Nonpayment of Rent

rules.title: Notice to Terminate Tenancy at Will and Right to Cure Nonpayment of Rent
rules.requirement: A landlord must give a tenant at will three months' written notice to terminate the tenancy (or, if rent is paid more often than every three months, notice equal to the rental interval or 30 days, whichever is longer). For nonpayment of rent, only 14 days' written notice to quit is required, but if the tenant has not received a similar nonpayment notice in the preceding 12 months, the tenant may cure by paying the full rent due within 10 days of receiving the notice, and the notice itself must contain specific statutory language informing the tenant of this right.
rules.key_value: 14 days' notice to quit (nonpayment); 10-day cure right; 3 months' notice (at-will termination)
rules.exemptions: If the notice fails to include the required statutory cure-right language, the tenant's time to pay or tender rent is extended to the day the answer is due in the landlord's possession action; also, if nonpayment was caused by a delay of a government agency in mailing a subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days and may treat the tenancy as not terminated if rent, interest, and costs are tendered within that time.
rules.quoted_span: In case of neglect or refusal to pay the rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the tenancy
rules.conflict_note: Section governs notice/cure procedure for terminating at-will tenancies generally; it does not establish 'just cause' requirements for eviction (Massachusetts is not a just-cause state statewide), so this record reflects notice and cure procedure rather than a substantive cause restriction.

rules.title: Required Disclosure Form Accompanying Notice to Quit for Nonpayment of Rent
rules.requirement: When a landlord gives a tenant a written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent, the notice must be accompanied by a state-developed form disclosing any repayment agreements, information on rental assistance programs and legal protections, and a prominent statement that the notice is not an eviction and the tenant is entitled to a court proceeding before being forced to leave. Courts may not accept an eviction filing for nonpayment of rent without proof this form was delivered to the tenant.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to residential dwelling unit evictions for nonpayment of rent only.

rules.quoted_span: No court having jurisdiction over an action for summary process pursuant to chapter 239, including the Boston municipal court department, shall, in an eviction for nonpayment of rent for a residential dwelling unit, accept for filing a writ, summons or complaint without proof of delivery of the form required under this section.
rules.conflict_note: This section governs notice/disclosure procedure for nonpayment-of-rent evictions rather than establishing substantive just-cause grounds for eviction generally; Massachusetts does not have a general just-cause eviction requirement, so this record is included only because it is a mandatory eviction-notice protection within the 'notice' scope of this category.
rules.penalty: Court may not accept the eviction filing (writ, summons or complaint) without proof of delivery of the required form.

rules.title: Statewide ban on local rent control, with narrow local opt-in exception
rules.requirement: Massachusetts cities and towns are barred from enacting or enforcing rent control. A city or town may only adopt rent control if it formally accepts this chapter, and even then compliance becomes entirely voluntary for property owners after six months, the regulation cannot apply to units owned by an entity with fewer than ten rental units or with fair market rent over $400, and the municipality must compensate owners for the gap between market and controlled rent out of its general funds.
rules.key_value: Exempts units owned by entities with <10 rental units or fair market rent >$400; after 6 months compliance is voluntary

coverage_conditions.notes: Exemption keyed to the number of rental units an owning person/entity holds (fewer than ten) or to fair market rent exceeding $400 per unit, not to a specific building's unit count.

rules.exemptions: Units owned by a person/entity owning fewer than ten rental units; units with fair market rent exceeding $400; after six months from initial adoption, compliance by property owners is voluntary. Local rent control regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties from regulation.
rules.interaction: Operates as a statewide preemption: local rent control is prohibited by default, and a city or town can only adopt it by affirmatively accepting this chapter, subject to the stated limits and compensation requirement.
rules.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides

rules.title: Security Deposit Cap, Handling, and Optional Fee-in-Lieu
rules.requirement: A landlord may not require a security deposit greater than the first month's rent, and the deposit must be placed in an interest-bearing bank account in Massachusetts, accompanied by a written statement of the premises' condition, and returned (with interest) within 30 days after tenancy ends, subject to itemized deductions for unpaid rent/taxes or tenant-caused damage. As of an August 1, 2025 amendment, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities may also authorize a landlord and tenant to agree to a recurring or scheduled fee in lieu of a deposit instead, but the fee must be optional, cannot be set based on the tenant's income, race, gender, disability, immigration status, household size or credit score, and the combined total of any such fee plus any deposit actually paid cannot exceed one month's rent.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent (deposit cap); fee-in-lieu alternative also capped at 1 month's rent combined total

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to residential tenancies generally; excludes vacation/recreational tenancies of 100 days or less. No building size, age, or ownership-based coverage conditions stated.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less for a vacation or recreational purpose. Fee-in-lieu option requires EOHLC regulations and is optional for both landlord and tenant, who may opt back into paying the full deposit instead.
rules.interaction: The fee-in-lieu mechanism (added effective 2025-08-01) operates alongside, not instead of, the underlying 1-month-rent deposit cap; a lessor who fails to comply with deposit-handling rules (e.g., separate account, timely itemized return) forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit.
rules.quoted_span: a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2)
rules.conflict_note: Document shows two versions of clause (1)(b)'s introductory text: one effective until August 1, 2025 and one as amended effective August 1, 2025; the underlying 1-month deposit cap is unchanged between versions, only the fee-in-lieu authorization and 'agent of the lessor' language were added.
rules.penalty: Lessor forfeits right to retain deposit for noncompliance; tenant may recover treble damages plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees for wrongful withholding or failure to pay required interest.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Bans landlords from using, paying for, or facilitating an algorithmic 'coordinator' (software or device) that collects competitively sensitive data (prices, lease terms, security deposits, occupancy levels) from multiple rental property owners to set or recommend rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Also bans two or more rental property owners from engaging in tacit or express 'parallel pricing coordination' on rents, and makes any violation a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act.
rules.exemptions: Does not cover: spreadsheets that operate without AI and require human analysis; databases that only query unprocessed stored data; use of data solely for research/statistical analysis/testing not used to set prices; publicly available free rent estimate tools; real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms to subscribers that do not set/recommend prices or collect competitively sensitive information; and government entities setting/limiting rents through affordability controls (e.g., Section 8, rent control/leveling ordinances, NJHMFA programs).
rules.interaction: Does not limit application of sections 6 through 17 of the New Jersey Antitrust Act to violations of this act, and is construed as in addition to that act and any other law. A municipality is prohibited from enacting an ordinance that conflicts with this act, though ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law remain permitted.
rules.quoted_span:
a coordinator to facilitate a tacit or express
agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition with respect
to residential dwelling units, including by performing a coordinating
function
rules.penalty: Violation is deemed a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, P.L.1970, c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.); the Attorney General must maintain a complaint intake location and may adopt implementing rules and regulations.

rules.title: Cap on Residential Rental Application Fees
rules.requirement: A landlord or their agent cannot charge an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental dwelling that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted annually for inflation (CPI) and published by the Division of Consumer Affairs.
rules.key_value: $50 (adjusted annually by CPI)

coverage_conditions.notes: Exempts dwelling units in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent, and exempts licensees of the NJ Real Estate Commission unless the licensee is itself the landlord of the property.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to: (1) a dwelling unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent; or (2) a licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate Commission, unless the licensee is the landlord of the property.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
rules.conflict_note: Enacted as P.L.2025, c.405 (A4899 4R) but approved January 20, 2026; effective date computed as the first day of the fourth month following enactment (May 1, 2026).
rules.penalty: Up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for each subsequent offense, enforced via summary proceedings under the Penalty Enforcement Law of 1999 (P.L.1999, c.274); amounts wrongfully charged are remitted to the applicant/prospective tenant.

rules.title: Good-Cause Eviction Protections for Rooming and Boarding House Residents
rules.requirement: Owners of rooming and boarding houses must follow the same good-cause and notice requirements as the general Eviction Law when evicting residents, unless the Department's Bureau of Rooming and Boarding House Standards orders otherwise.

coverage_conditions.notes: Rooming or boarding house: a building with at least two living units occupied by unrelated persons without private kitchens and bathrooms (N.J.S.A. 55:13B-3), subject to statutory exceptions (e.g., hotels with more than 85% temporary occupancy, school/college dormitories, buildings housing only college students, certain disability residences).

rules.exemptions: Bureau of Rooming and Boarding House Standards may order otherwise; statutory exceptions under the Rooming and Boarding House Act (hotels with >85% temporary occupancy, dormitories, certain residences for the disabled) remove a building from 'rooming/boarding house' status entirely.
rules.interaction: Incorporates by reference the good-cause and notice requirements of the general Eviction Law (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.); also requires at least 3 working days' notice to the County Welfare Board before starting an eviction action for any resident (N.J.A.C. 5:26-3.4(c)).
rules.quoted_span:
require owners of rooming and boarding houses to follow the good causes and notice requirements 
of the Eviction Law when evicting residents, except if otherwise ordered by the Bureau

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act – Good Cause Required for Residential Eviction
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a residential tenant only for one of the statutory good causes (e.g., nonpayment of rent, disorderly conduct, property damage, substantial lease violation, owner retirement of the property from residential use, conversion to condominium/cooperative, certain criminal convictions on the premises). Except for nonpayment of rent, each cause must be described in a written Notice to Quit (sometimes preceded by a Notice to Cease), with required notice periods ranging from 3 days to 18 months depending on the cause, before an eviction suit may be filed. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy must receive relocation assistance equal to six times their monthly rent before they can be removed.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit periods range from 3 days to 18 months depending on cause; relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy eviction = 6 times monthly rent

coverage_conditions.notes: Does not apply to hotel, motel, or guest-house transient/seasonal guests unless the occupant has no alternate residence and resides there on a continual basis; does not apply to a unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it.

rules.exemptions: Two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotel/motel/guest-house transient or seasonal guests (unless no alternate residence and continual occupancy); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies the unit.
rules.interaction: Applies to most residential rentals including single-family homes, mobile homes, apartment buildings/complexes, and rooming/boarding homes.
rules.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

rules.title: Just-Cause Eviction Rules for Owner-Occupied Two- and Three-Family Dwellings
rules.requirement: In owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings, a tenant can only be removed by court order, and only for specific causes: staying after lease expiration, failing to pay rent, disorderly conduct destroying other tenants' peace and quiet, willful destruction/damage, constant violation of written rules, or violating a lease re-entry provision. Required notice to quit varies by tenancy type and cause.
rules.key_value: Notice to quit: none required for nonpayment of rent; 3-day notice for disorderly/destructive/rule-violation causes; 1 month for month-to-month tenancy; 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancy

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies specifically to landlord-occupied (owner-occupied) two- and three-family dwellings.

rules.exemptions: Applies only to owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings; larger or non-owner-occupied buildings are covered instead by the general Anti-Eviction Act causes.
rules.interaction: Narrower subset of just-cause grounds than the general Anti-Eviction Act (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1), applicable specifically to small owner-occupied buildings.
rules.quoted_span:
Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when 
a court issues an order for eviction.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act
rules.requirement: Qualifying senior citizens (62+ before conversion recording), permanently disabled persons, or disabled veterans (60%+ service-connected disability) who have lived in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership for at least one year before the conversion recording may be protected from eviction for up to 40 years, provided their household income does not exceed the greater of three times the county average per-person income or $50,000.
rules.key_value: Up to 40 years protected tenancy; income cap = greater of 3x county average per-person income or $50,000

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to buildings being converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership; tenant must have resided in the building at least 1 year prior to the conversion recording date.

rules.exemptions: Tenants in Hudson County who do not qualify under this Act may be eligible for additional protected tenancy under the separate Tenant Protection Act of 1992.
rules.interaction: Applications for protected tenancy generally must be filed within 60 days, though later filings may be accepted for good reason if conversion has not yet occurred; a related Tenant Protection Act of 1992 extends similar protection in Hudson County to tenants who do not qualify under this Act.
rules.quoted_span:
Tenants may be protected from eviction for 40 years 
if their family income is not more than three (3) times the average per person income in their 
county or $50,000.00, whichever  is greater

rules.title: Good Cause Required to Evict or Fail to Renew Lease (Anti-Eviction Act)
rules.requirement: A landlord of residential rental property may not refuse to renew a tenant's lease or evict a tenant without good cause, as defined by the statute's list of permitted grounds for eviction. This protection does not apply to owner-occupied buildings of two or three units, motels, hotels, or transient or seasonal units.

coverage_conditions.notes: Does not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, or transient/seasonal units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings, motels, hotels, and transient or seasonal units are excluded (see separate rules for owner-occupied two/three-family dwelling evictions).
rules.quoted_span:
No landlord of residential rental properties except t hose in owner occupied two or three 
family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient, or seasonal units may fail to renew any lease, 
regardless of whether it is written or oral unless they have good cause not to renew the lease.
rules.conflict_note: The guide cites this provision as '(N.J.S.A. 2A:18:61.3)' with colons rather than the standard 'N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3' hyphen format used elsewhere; treated as the same section.

rules.title: Penalties for Bad-Faith Owner Move-In / Demolition Evictions
rules.requirement: If a landlord evicts a tenant on the ground of wanting to personally occupy the unit, the landlord must actually occupy it for at least six months, or else owes the former tenant treble damages plus attorney fees and costs. If a landlord evicts a tenant to permanently board up, demolish, or retire a building from residential use, the landlord cannot return any unit to residential use for five years, or else owes treble damages, attorney fees/costs, and a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation, and the property cannot be registered as a planned real estate development during that five-year period.
rules.key_value: 6-month personal-occupancy requirement; 5-year residential-use restriction after demolition/retirement notice; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation; treble damages plus attorney fees/costs

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to landlords who evict tenants on stated grounds of personal occupancy or permanent removal of the building from residential use.

rules.interaction: Operates as an anti-fraud backstop to the owner-occupancy and demolition/retirement 'good causes' for eviction under the Anti-Eviction Act.
rules.quoted_span:
When a tenant vacates a dwelling unit after having been given notice that the  landlord 
wishes to personally occupy the unit the landlord must occupy the unit for at least six (6) months.
rules.penalty: Treble (3x) damages plus attorney fees and costs; additionally, up to $10,000 civil penalty per violation and a 5-year bar on planned real estate development registration for the demolition/retirement scenario.

rules.title: Prohibition on Retaliatory (Reprisal) Eviction
rules.requirement: A landlord cannot evict a tenant, substantially alter the lease or its terms, or refuse to renew a lease in reprisal for the tenant exercising certain civil rights, such as enforcing lease or legal rights, making a good-faith health/safety complaint (after first notifying the landlord), or participating in a tenant organization.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to all rental properties used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are excluded from this reprisal protection.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord cannot take reprisal action against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of 
a lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when a tenant exercises certain civil rights
rules.penalty: Tenant may sue the landlord for damages in a civil action.

rules.title: Foreclosure Fairness Act – 90-Day Notice Before Eviction After Foreclosure
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. Before a tenant can be evicted due to foreclosure, the new owner who purchased the property and wants to personally occupy it as a primary residence must give the tenant a 90-day notice to quit; this notice may be given up to 90 days before an existing lease expires, and tenants with longer remaining leases cannot be evicted until the lease ends and the 90-day notice has also been given.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to residential tenants in properties undergoing or following foreclosure.

rules.exemptions: Month-to-month tenants and tenants in owner-occupied two- and three-family units are NOT exempt from the 90-day notice requirement.
rules.interaction: Supplements, and does not preempt, any State or local law providing longer notice periods or additional tenant protections in foreclosure; federal foreclosure law likewise does not preempt such State/local protections.
rules.quoted_span:
Before a tenant can be evicted due 
to foreclosure, the landlord must provide the tenant with a 90 -day notice to qui t when the 
foreclosed property has been purchased by a buyer who wants to personally occupy it as his or her 
primary residence.

rules.title: Landlord registration required before a tenant may be evicted
rules.requirement: A landlord must file a registration statement (with the municipal clerk for one- or two-family non-owner-occupied homes, or with the Bureau of Housing Inspection for buildings with three or more units). A landlord who has not properly registered is barred from evicting a tenant from the building.

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to non-owner-occupied one- or two-family homes and to buildings with three or more rental units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two-family homes are not required to be registered.
rules.interaction: If a landlord has failed to register, the court must reserve judgment and continue an eviction case for up to 90 days to allow time to comply; if the landlord still has not complied, the case must be dismissed.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord 
registration law prohibits a landlord from evicting a tenant in the building if the landlord has not 
been properly registered

rules.title: No statewide rent control; rent increases must not be unconscionable
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no state law that caps or controls rent, but municipalities may pass local rent control or rent-leveling ordinances. Where no local ordinance applies, a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rate, and the increase must not be unconscionable (so unreasonable as to shock the conscience).
rules.exemptions: Rents subject to a municipal rent control ordinance are governed by that ordinance instead. Newly constructed multiple dwellings and government-subsidized, HUD-insured, or NJHMFA-financed housing may be exempt from local rent control ordinances.
rules.interaction: Unconscionability is assessed case-by-case considering the size of the increase, landlord's expenses/profitability, comparable rents, bargaining position, and judicial discretion (Fromet Properties v. Buel; Hale v. Farrakhan). Local rent control/leveling ordinances, where enacted, take precedence over this general standard.
rules.quoted_span:
Although the State of New Jersey does not have any laws that establish, govern, or control 
rents, a landlord can increase rents if they follow certain procedures.

rules.title: No rent increase to cover condominium/cooperative conversion costs
rules.requirement: If a building is converted to condominium, cooperative, or fee-simple ownership, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. This prohibition applies to all tenants in the building regardless of protected-tenancy status.
rules.exemptions: Rents may still be increased to cover the cost of new services or amenities.
rules.quoted_span:
rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the 
conversion

rules.title: Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law - 30-year exemption from local rent control
rules.requirement: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinance for 30 years following completion of construction of the building.
rules.key_value: 30 years

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to newly constructed multiple dwellings; the exemption runs for 30 years from completion of construction.

rules.interaction: Rents subsidized by governmental funding may also be exempt from local rent control ordinances.
rules.quoted_span:
newly 
constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period 
of 30 years following completion of construction of the building

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination bars tenant screening based on source of lawful income
rules.requirement: Landlords and rental agencies may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise discriminate against, prospective tenants based on source of lawful income (such as housing vouchers or public assistance), along with race, creed, color, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, and other protected categories.

coverage_conditions.notes: Exempt: two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex residences as to familial status only.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, or residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex (e.g., YMCA, age-restricted housing), as it pertains to familial status.
rules.interaction: A landlord may still lawfully refuse an applicant for insufficient income, overcrowding that would violate zoning, or poor credit history under 42 U.S.C.A. §§ 3601-3610; violations of the Law Against Discrimination can result in fines up to $10,000 for a first offense under N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a).
rules.quoted_span:
requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, 
ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, 
affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, 
nationality, or source of lawful income
rules.penalty: Up to $10,000 for a first offense, plus potential monetary damages and an order to rent the unit to the complainant.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act — criminal record screening restrictions
rules.requirement: NJ housing providers cannot ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after making a conditional offer of tenancy (except methamphetamine-manufacturing convictions on federally assisted housing and lifetime sex-offender-registry status). After a conditional offer, a provider may only consider: certain serious violent/sexual felonies (no time limit), 1st-degree indictable offenses within the prior 6 years, 2nd/3rd-degree offenses within 4 years, and 4th-degree offenses within 1 year. Arrests without conviction, expunged or pardoned convictions, vacated convictions, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records can never be considered. A conditional offer may only be withdrawn based on a qualifying record if necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, following an individualized assessment and with written notice and appeal rights to the applicant.
rules.key_value: Lookback: permanent bar for enumerated violent/sexual felonies; 6 years (1st degree); 4 years (2nd/3rd degree); 1 year (4th degree)

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to any 'housing provider' (landlord, owner, lessor, sublessor, assignee or agent) renting a 'rental dwelling unit'; landlords who rent to or screen out applicants with criminal records in compliance with the act are granted civil immunity.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to owner-occupied premises of 4 or fewer dwelling units (excluded from definition of 'rental dwelling unit'); methamphetamine-manufacturing convictions on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime sex-offender-registry status may be asked about pre-offer; arrests/charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated, juvenile adjudications, and sealed records may never be considered.
rules.interaction: Enforced exclusively through administrative complaint to the Division on Civil Rights (no private court action); an applicant placed in a unit via a director's order may be evicted, notwithstanding the Anti-Eviction Act, P.L.1974, c.49 (C.2A:18-61.1 et seq.), with 45 days' notice if the housing provider later wins an appeal overturning the violation finding.
rules.quoted_span:
a.  A housing provider shall not, either before
or after the issuance of a conditional offer, evaluate an applicant based on
any of the following types of criminal records:
rules.penalty: Civil penalty enforced by the Division on Civil Rights: up to $1,000 for a first violation in 5 years, up to $5,000 for a second within 5 years, up to $10,000 for three-plus within 7 years; director may also order return of application fee, cease-and-desist, or (where feasible) issuance of a conditional offer/comparable unit.

rules.title: Security deposit must be returned within 30 days of tenancy termination
rules.requirement: Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned, less lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear or other money owed under the lease, sent by personal delivery, registered, or certified mail along with an itemized list of any deductions.
rules.key_value: 30 days
rules.exemptions: No deductions may be made from the security deposit of a tenant who remains in possession of the rental premises. A shortened 5-business-day return period applies when a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation.
rules.interaction: Interest earned on the deposit must separately be paid or credited to the tenant under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19(c); failure to pay required interest or give notice lets the tenant apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest toward rent under N.J.S.A. 46:8-19.1(c).
rules.quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant
rules.penalty: If the landlord fails to timely return the deposit, or the tenant disputes a deduction, the tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

rules.title: Security Deposit Law — maximum deposit and annual increase cap
rules.requirement: A New Jersey landlord is not required to collect a security deposit, but if one is collected it cannot exceed one and one-half times one month's rent (combined with any pet deposit), and any yearly increase to the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit amount. Prepaid rent (including last month's rent) counts toward this cap, so total upfront charges (security deposit plus first month's rent) cannot exceed two and one-half times the monthly rent.
rules.key_value: max 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase cap 10% of current deposit

coverage_conditions.notes: Applies to most residential rental properties including mobile homes; owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt, though a tenant there may opt in 30 days after written request to the landlord.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant requests coverage in writing (effective 30 days later). Seasonal use/rental (125 days or fewer) is exempt from the trust-account investment provisions.
rules.interaction: Advance rent payments (including last month's rent), however labeled, are treated as part of the security deposit and count toward the 1.5x cap per Brownstone Arms v. Asher and Reilly v. Weiss.
rules.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional 
yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

rules.title: Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Landlords may not use an algorithmic device (software that uses nonpublic competitor data to recommend rental rates or occupancy levels) to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property in San Diego. It is also unlawful for anyone to sell, license, or otherwise provide such a device to a landlord.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to software that publishes reports on rental rates/occupancy from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data that is more than 90 days old (or from publicly available information) and does not recommend future rates/occupancy; also does not apply to software used to set rental rates or income limits under local, state, or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates
or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.conflict_note: Document is a staff report and draft ordinance (O-2025-107) with the ordinance number and date of final passage left blank, indicating it had not yet been adopted by Council as of this document (introduced ~Feb 2025); status recorded as pending based on the document itself since no later enactment confirmation was available for verification.
rules.penalty: A tenant may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation in a civil action against the landlord; each month of a continuing violation and each affected property counts as a separate violation; a prevailing tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and lease provisions barring recovery of attorney's fees are unenforceable as to such claims.

rules.title: Just Cause Required for Termination of Tenancy
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a residential tenancy covered by this Division without just cause, which must be either an at-fault cause (e.g., nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to renew a substantially similar lease, criminal activity/threats, unauthorized sublet, refusal of entry, unlawful use, holdover employee-occupant, failure to surrender after notice) or a no-fault cause (owner/family move-in for at least 12 continuous months, withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with a government habitability/vacate order, or demolition/substantial remodel).

coverage_conditions.notes: Division does not apply to: transient/tourist hotel occupancy; short-term residential occupancy; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing for very low/low/moderate income (Section 8 tenants remain covered); mobilehomes under the state Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, licensed elder/adult care facilities, and non-profit transitional housing; school/college dormitories; residential property where the tenant shares bath/kitchen with a resident landlord; a single-family home or duplex unit occupied by the landlord as principal residence (landlord renting out no more than two bedrooms/ADUs, or one unit of a two-unit structure); housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); and certain non-corporate-owned stand-alone rental properties where tenants received the required exemption notice.

rules.exemptions: See coverage_conditions; the alienable-property exception additionally requires the landlord NOT be a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, and that tenants receive written notice of the exemption.
